# Chern Characters of Canonical Generators on the K-homology of $SU_q(2)$

## Introduction and Motivation

This paper is devoted to a careful and rigorous examination of certain remarks and conjectures originally formulated in \cite{G2}, concerning the interplay between K-homological invariants and the quantum group structure of $SU_q(2)$. While the earlier reference sketched key ideas and stated important results, several assertions were left without full proof, and at least one significant conjecture remained open. The present work fills these gaps, providing complete arguments and thereby placing the theory on a firmer foundation.

## Detailed Proof of the Chern Character Remark

The first main contribution of this paper is to supply a complete and detailed proof of a remark stated in \cite{G2} regarding the Chern characters associated to the canonical generators of the K-homology group of $SU_q(2)$. In the original reference, this statement was presented without a full derivation, leaving open the precise mechanisms by which these Chern characters are computed and behave under the natural symmetries of the quantum group. Here, we reconstruct the argument from first principles, carefully tracking the relevant pairings between K-homology classes and cyclic cohomology, and verifying at each stage that the constructions are consistent with the noncommutative geometric framework underlying $SU_q(2)$.

## Non-Invariance Under the $SU_q(2)$ Coaction

A central and somewhat unexpected result established in this work is that the Chern characters of these canonical generators fail to be invariant under the natural coaction of $SU_q(2)$ on itself. This is a noteworthy finding, since one might naively expect that objects constructed canonically from the K-homology of a quantum group should respect the symmetry encoded by the coaction, in analogy with classical situations where equivariant cohomological invariants often exhibit such invariance. Our detailed computations show that this expectation does not hold in the quantum setting: the Chern characters transform nontrivially under the coaction, revealing a genuine asymmetry that distinguishes the noncommutative case from its classical counterpart. This result underscores the subtlety of equivariance phenomena in the noncommutative geometry of quantum groups and highlights the need for careful analysis rather than reliance on classical intuition.

## Resolution of the Conjecture on the Twisted Chern Character

The second major result of this paper addresses a conjecture posed in \cite{G2} concerning the twisted Chern character arising from an odd equivariant spectral triple on $SU_q(2)$. This spectral triple, constructed to encode equivariant Dirac-type operator data compatible with the quantum group symmetry, gives rise to a twisted Chern character via the associated Connes–Chern pairing in a twisted cyclic cohomology theory. The conjecture from \cite{G2} asserted, without proof, that this twisted Chern character should be nontrivial—a statement of considerable importance, since the nontriviality of such an invariant would confirm that the odd equivariant spectral triple genuinely detects nontrivial K-homological information about $SU_q(2)$.

In this paper, we settle this conjecture affirmatively. Through an explicit and rigorous computation of the relevant pairing, we demonstrate that the twisted Chern character associated to the odd equivariant spectral triple is indeed nontrivial. This resolves the open question left by \cite{G2} and confirms that the spectral triple in question provides a nontrivial and meaningful equivariant K-homological invariant for the quantum group $SU_q(2)$.

## Contributions and Significance

Taken together, these results make substantial contributions to the broader program of understanding noncommutative geometric structures associated with quantum groups. By providing complete proofs where only sketches previously existed, by uncovering the failure of invariance under the natural coaction, and by rigorously confirming the nontriviality of the twisted Chern character, this work deepens our understanding of the equivariant K-homology and cyclic cohomology theory of $SU_q(2)$. These findings not only clarify specific technical points left open in \cite{G2}, but also illuminate more general features of equivariance and symmetry breaking in the noncommutative geometric setting, contributing valuable insights to the ongoing development of quantum group theory and its interaction with index theory and spectral triples.

# On the Equivariance of Chern Characters for $SU_q(2)$ and the Nontriviality of the Twisted Chern Character

## 1. Introduction

The quantum group $SU_q(2)$, for $q\in(0,1)$, has served for over two decades as the primary testing ground for ideas in noncommutative differential geometry that go beyond the classical framework of spin manifolds. Its coordinate algebra $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ carries a rich supply of $K$-theoretic and $K$-homological data: the fundamental representation gives rise to a canonical class in $K_0$, and the Dirac-type operators constructed by Chakraborty–Pal, and subsequently refined by Dąbrowski–Sitarz and others, produce equivariant Fredholm modules and spectral triples representing generators of $K$-homology.

A basic question in equivariant noncommutative geometry is whether the pairing between $K$-theory and $K$-homology, or more refined invariants such as the Chern character, behave well with respect to the natural coaction of $SU_q(2)$ on itself. In the classical case of a compact Lie group $G$ acting on itself by translation, the analogous question is answered trivially: characteristic classes computed via the Chern–Weil construction are of course invariant under left translation, since translation acts transitively and by isometries on the group manifold. One might naively expect an analogous invariance to persist in the $q$-deformed setting, at least at the level of cohomology classes represented by cyclic cocycles obtained from the Chern character of a $K$-homology class.

In \cite{G2}, it was asserted — without proof — that this naive expectation *fails*: the Chern character of the canonical generator of $K_0(SU_q(2))$ (equivalently, of the fundamental class in $K$-homology dual to the spectral triple of Chakraborty–Pal) is **not** invariant under the natural coaction
$$
\Delta: \mathcal{A}(SU_q(2)) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(SU_q(2)) \otimes \mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))
$$
in the sense that the associated cyclic cocycle, pulled back via a coaction on the relevant cyclic cohomology complex, fails to agree with the original cocycle up to coboundary in a way compatible with the comultiplication structure. This assertion, while stated in \cite{G2}, was left without a detailed proof, and its justification requires a careful analysis of the interplay between the modular properties of the Haar state, the twisted commutation relations satisfied by the generators $a, b, a^*, b^*$ of $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$, and the explicit form of the Chern–Connes character associated with a finitely summable Fredholm module.

The present paper has two principal aims.

**First**, we supply the missing proof of the non-invariance claim of \cite{G2}. We do this by working explicitly with the odd and even Fredholm modules constructed from the equivariant spectral triples on $SU_q(2)$, computing the relevant Chern character cocycles in low degree using the basis of matrix coefficients $t^l_{m,n}$ of irreducible corepresentations, and exhibiting an explicit obstruction to invariance under the coaction. The obstruction is traced to the appearance of modular twisting factors $q^{2(m+n)}$ arising from the non-cocommutativity of the coproduct and the non-unimodularity of the associated Haar functional's modular automorphism, which do not cancel against the corresponding factors appearing in the definition of the equivariant Chern character. We show that this failure of invariance is not a pathology of a particular choice of cocycle representative, but persists in cohomology: the difference of the two natural cocycles represents a nonzero class in the relevant $(b,B)$-bicomplex.

**Second**, we resolve affirmatively a conjecture left open in \cite{G2} concerning the **twisted Chern character** associated with an *odd* equivariant spectral triple on $SU_q(2)$. Such a spectral triple, of the type constructed by Chakraborty and Pal using the operator $D$ acting on a suitable Hilbert space completion of $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ with respect to the Haar state, is not finitely summable in the naive sense, and the ordinary Chern–Connes character construction must be replaced by Connes–Moscovici-type twisted cyclic cohomology built from a modular automorphism $\sigma$ of the underlying algebra. The conjecture of \cite{G2} asserts that the resulting twisted Chern character, an element of twisted cyclic cohomology $HC^{\bullet}_{\sigma}(\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2)))$, is *nontrivial*, i.e., does not vanish in twisted cyclic cohomology and hence provides genuine new information about the noncommutative geometry of $SU_q(2)$ beyond what is captured by the index pairing alone. We prove this conjecture by an explicit computation of the pairing of the twisted Chern character with a distinguished idempotent representing a generator of equivariant $K$-theory, showing that this pairing is a nonzero rational function of $q$, thereby forcing nontriviality of the cohomology class.

## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1 The algebra $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$

Fix $q \in (0,1)$. Recall that $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ is the $*$-algebra generated by elements $a, b$ subject to the relations
$$
ab = q\, ba, \qquad ab^* = q\, b^*a, \qquad bb^* = b^*b,
$$
$$
a^*a + q^2 b^*b = 1, \qquad aa^* + bb^* = 1,
$$
with $*$ the involution determined by $a^*, b^*$ being the adjoints of $a, b$. The comultiplication
$$
\Delta(a) = a\otimes a - q\, b^* \otimes b, \qquad \Delta(b) = b\otimes a + a^*\otimes b
$$
makes $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ into a Hopf $*$-algebra, and there is a unique Haar state $h$ satisfying $(h\otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta = (\mathrm{id}\otimes h)\Delta = h(\cdot)1$.

The irreducible corepresentations are indexed by $l \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, with matrix coefficients $t^l_{m,n}$, $-l \leq m,n \leq l$, forming a linear basis of $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ (the Peter–Weyl decomposition). The Haar state satisfies the orthogonality relations
$$
h\big((t^l_{m,n})^* t^{l'}_{m',n'}\big) = \delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}\delta_{nn'} \frac{q^{2n}}{[2l+1]_q} \cdot (\text{normalization factor}),
$$
reflecting the fact that $h$ is a KMS state with a nontrivial modular automorphism group
$$
\sigma_t(a) = q^{-2it} a, \qquad \sigma_t(b) = b, \qquad \sigma_t(a^*) = q^{2it}a^*, \qquad \sigma_t(b^*) = b^*.
$$
This modular twisting is the essential source of the noninvariance phenomena studied below; in the classical limit $q \to 1$ the modular group becomes trivial and all the invariance statements of the classical theory are recovered.

### 2.2 The equivariant spectral triple

Following Chakraborty–Pal, one represents $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}) \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$ (in the odd case) via an explicit combination of shift and diagonal operators built from the Peter–Weyl basis, and defines a self-adjoint operator $D$ with discrete spectrum growing like $q^{-|n|}$ so that $[D, x]$ is bounded for all $x$ in a dense subalgebra, and $(1+D^2)^{-s/2}$ is trace-class for $s$ sufficiently large. The resulting triple $(\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2)), \mathcal{H}, D)$ is equivariant with respect to the coaction of $SU_q(2)$ on itself, in the sense that there is a corepresentation $U$ of $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))$ on $\mathcal{H}$ intertwining the actions appropriately, and $D$ commutes with $U$ (or anticommutes, in a graded sense, in the even case).

This equivariant spectral triple represents the fundamental generator of the $K$-homology group $K^1(SU_q(2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ (odd case) or $K^0(SU_q(2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ (even case, using the two spectral triples of opposite chirality constructed by Dąbrowski–Sitarz and Chakraborty–Pal).

### 2.3 The Chern character and its equivariant analogue

For a $(2n+1)$-summable odd Fredholm module $(\mathcal{H}, F)$ over an algebra $\mathcal{A}$, the Chern character is the cyclic cocycle
$$
\mathrm{ch}^{2n+1}(a_0, \dots, a_{2n+1}) = \lambda_n\, \mathrm{Tr}\big(\gamma\, F[F,a_0][F,a_1]\cdots[F,a_{2n+1}]\big),
$$
for an appropriate normalization constant $\lambda_n$, where $F = D|D|^{-1}$. This defines a class in $HC^{2n+1}(\mathcal{A})$, and the pairing with $K_1(\mathcal{A})$ recovers the Fredholm index pairing.

An **equivariant** version of this construction, as proposed in \cite{G2}, seeks to lift $\mathrm{ch}^{\bullet}$ to a cocycle valued in $\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2))\otimes HC^{\bullet}(\mathcal{A}(SU_q(2)))$ or, dually, to ask that the ordinary Chern character cocycle $\varphi = \mathrm{ch}^{2n+1}$ satisfy a coinvariance relation of the schematic form
$$
(\Delta \otimes \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(2n+1)})\, \varphi \; \overset{?}{=} \; 1 \otimes \varphi
$$
after appropriate identifications, generalizing the classical statement that left-translation-invariant differential forms remain invariant under further translation. The question addressed in \cite{G2}, and answered with full proof here, is whether such a relation can hold at the level of cyclic cohomology classes.

# Understanding Chern Classes in Modern Geometry

Chern classes represent one of the most profound contributions to differential geometry and topology, named after the mathematician Shiing-Shen Chern who developed this theory in the 1940s. These characteristic classes provide a powerful tool for understanding the topological properties of complex vector bundles, bridging the gap between algebraic geometry, differential topology, and theoretical physics.

At its core, a Chern class assigns cohomology classes to complex vector bundles, capturing essential information about how these bundles twist and turn over their base manifolds. The theory begins with the first Chern class, which measures the obstruction to finding a global nonvanishing section of a line bundle. This seemingly simple invariant carries enormous geometric significance, appearing in contexts ranging from the classification of holomorphic line bundles to the computation of intersection numbers on algebraic varieties.

Furthermore, the complete hierarchy of Chern classes—not just the first one—provides a comprehensive framework for classifying vector bundles up to certain equivalences. The total Chern class, expressed as a formal sum of individual Chern classes, satisfies elegant properties such as the Whitney sum formula, which describes how these classes behave under direct sums of bundles. This multiplicative structure makes Chern classes remarkably computable in practice, even for complicated geometric situations.

The applications of Chern class theory extend far beyond pure mathematics. In theoretical physics, particularly in gauge theory and string theory, Chern classes appear naturally when studying anomalies, characteristic numbers, and topological invariants of physical field configurations. The Chern-Simons theory, for instance, has become fundamental to our understanding of three-dimensional topological quantum field theories and has found surprising connections to condensed matter physics, particularly in the study of topological insulators.

Furthermore, Chern classes play a crucial role in the celebrated Atiyah-Singer index theorem, which relates analytical properties of differential operators to topological invariants of the underlying manifold. This theorem, one of the most significant results in twentieth-century mathematics, demonstrates how Chern classes serve as a bridge connecting seemingly disparate areas of mathematics—analysis, topology, and geometry—into a unified conceptual framework.

The enduring importance of Chern's work lies not only in its technical sophistication but in its unifying power, revealing deep connections between algebra, geometry, and analysis that continue to inspire new mathematical discoveries today.
